name: Wöhler's Urea Synthesis
statement: Wöhler made urea, a compound of living things, from an inorganic salt, unsettling the idea of a vital force.
statementAccent: unsettling the idea of a vital force
meaning: Wöhler's urea synthesis was the 1828 preparation of urea, an organic compound found in urine, from an inorganic starting material by the German chemist Friedrich Wöhler, an experiment traditionally cited as a landmark in the history of chemistry. Attempting to make ammonium cyanate, an inorganic salt, Wöhler found that on heating it he obtained urea instead, the two substances being isomers with the same atoms arranged differently. The significance usually attached to this is that it challenged vitalism, the long-standing doctrine that organic compounds, the substances of living things, could be produced only by living organisms possessing a special vital force, and could not be synthesized from ordinary inorganic matter. By making an organic compound from an inorganic one in the laboratory, Wöhler appeared to breach the supposed divide between the living and non-living realms of chemistry, and his synthesis is often called a beginning of modern organic chemistry. In a famous letter to his teacher Berzelius, Wöhler wrote that he could make urea without the use of kidneys of any animal, be it man or dog. Modern historians, however, regard the story that this single experiment killed vitalism at a stroke as an oversimplified myth, since vitalism declined gradually over decades.
mechanism: The experiment rests on the chemical fact that two compounds with the same composition can differ in the arrangement of their atoms, and that heating can convert one into the other. Wöhler was working with cyanate salts and set out to prepare ammonium cyanate by combining an ammonium compound with cyanate. Ammonium cyanate and urea have exactly the same chemical formula, the same numbers of carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, and oxygen atoms, but arranged into different structures, making them isomers. When Wöhler heated the solution in which he expected ammonium cyanate to form, the atoms rearranged, and what crystallized out was not the inorganic salt he intended but urea, a well-known organic product of animal metabolism. He identified the substance as urea by comparing its properties with urea obtained from urine and found them identical. The transformation is essentially an internal rearrangement of ammonium cyanate into urea driven by heat. The importance claimed for it lay not in the chemistry of the rearrangement itself but in its implication: an organic compound had been produced from a starting material regarded as inorganic, without the involvement of any living organism or its supposed vital force.

whyItMatters: Wöhler's urea synthesis is one of the most famous experiments in the history of chemistry, traditionally celebrated as the moment that began to break down the barrier between organic and inorganic chemistry and to undermine vitalism, the doctrine that the compounds of living things could be made only by living organisms endowed with a special vital force. By synthesizing urea, unmistakably an organic compound, from a starting material regarded as inorganic, Wöhler suggested that organic substances obey the same chemistry as everything else and can be built in the laboratory, an idea foundational to the vast field of organic chemistry and to the later synthesis of countless natural and artificial compounds. The experiment is a staple of chemistry education and a symbol of the unity of chemistry across the living and non-living worlds. It is equally valuable, however, as a case study in the history of science, because the popular narrative that Wöhler killed vitalism in a single stroke is now recognized as a myth: vitalism actually declined slowly over decades through the work of many chemists, and Wöhler himself did not frame his result as a crusade. As both a landmark synthesis and a lesson about how science really changes, Wöhler's urea synthesis remains important.

limits: Wöhler's urea synthesis is real and important, but the dramatic story usually told about it is oversimplified and should be qualified. Historians of science emphasize that the claim that this one experiment killed vitalism at a stroke is a myth: vitalism was already being eroded and continued to decline gradually over decades, with later syntheses such as Kolbe's work in the 1840s doing more to dislodge it, and Wöhler himself did not present his result as a decisive blow against vitalism, being more interested in the phenomenon of isomerism. There is even a debated point about whether the ammonium cyanate he used traced back in part to organically derived materials, which some critics raised, so that too should be presented as contested rather than settled. The precise wording of his letter to Berzelius survives in translation.
misreadings: Wöhler's urea synthesis did not single-handedly destroy vitalism; historians regard that story as a myth, since vitalism declined gradually over decades and Wöhler did not frame his work as a decisive blow. He did not set out to make urea, but obtained it accidentally while aiming for ammonium cyanate. And the experiment showed a chemical rearrangement of isomers, not a magical creation of life's substance, so treating it as instantly killing vitalism, as a deliberate synthesis of urea, or as bridging life and non-life at a stroke, misreads a genuine but mythologized landmark of chemistry.
origin: The 1828 synthesis of urea from ammonium cyanate by the German chemist Friedrich Wöhler, traditionally cited as a landmark against vitalism and a beginning of organic chemistry, though its role in ending vitalism is now seen as mythologized.
